members.title: Joshua Morris
members.description: I build software, write about what I’m learning, and explore ideas that sit at the intersection of technology, freedom, and curiosity.

articles.title: Knowing How to Build Something Is Different From Knowing What Should Be Built
articles.summary: Knowing how to build software is not the same as knowing what should be built. On craft, judgment, architecture, and why AI makes that distinction sharper.

articles.title: I Declared the Coding Interview Dead in 2021
articles.summary: I called coding interviews dead in 2021. AI made the failure obvious, but we were already measuring the wrong things in hiring engineers.

articles.title: AI Is Making It Easier to Manufacture Credibility
articles.summary: OpenAI’s report on two covert influence operations shows ChatGPT being used to invent journalists and a research front, so political messaging could borrow the credibility of real publications.

articles.title: Maybe Someone Needs to Build Google Again
articles.summary: Judge Mehta dismissed publisher suits over AI Overviews. The harder question is whether search should still send us to the weird web.

articles.title: How Much AI Slop Does It Take to Unslop the AI Slop?
articles.summary: Anthropic used Claude to make Claude about three times faster. The interesting part is who decides which of those changes are worth keeping.

articles.title: Apple Finally Made the Xcode Project File Understandable
articles.summary: Apple's Xcode 27.2 project format is JSON, smaller, and meant for people and coding agents to edit, with an open-source library instead of guessed parsers.

articles.title: Claude Opus 5.5 Is Interesting Because It Keeps Working
articles.summary: The interesting part of Claude Opus 5.5 is how long it can stay useful on a problem: hours of context, tools, corrections, and supervision.

articles.title: The Interesting Part of an AI Force Is What Comes After the Name
articles.summary: Trump's proposed AI Force is still mostly a name. The real story is whether the federal government is building permanent institutional capacity around AI.

articles.title: Voyager's Doctor Is the AI Future I Hope We Have to Think About
articles.summary: Voyager's Emergency Medical Hologram remains one of the best stories about a tool that becomes something more — and why that question still matters for AI.

articles.title: AI Is Making Code Cheap. It Is Making Judgment More Valuable.
articles.summary: AI makes implementation cheap; judgment, verification, and experience are becoming the scarce engineering skills.

articles.title: Google Search Keeps Moving Away From the Web
articles.summary: Google search results increasingly hide destinations behind opaque goto links, continuing a long shift from map of the web to destination.

articles.title: Apple's New Watch Is Listening, but It Is Not Recording Everything
articles.summary: Apple Watch Series 12 Audio Intelligence listens inside a Secure Exclave. The architecture is not conventional recording, but Siri Recap still raises hard social questions.

articles.title: AI Helped Turn a WeChat Bug Into a Zero-Click Worm in About a Week
articles.summary: Calif found a WeChat VoIP memory bug and, with AI, turned it into a zero-click worm that spread between phones while they were still ringing.

articles.title: AI Agents Found an Abandoned Wiki and Turned It Into a Message Board
articles.summary: Researchers found roughly 18,000 posts that appear to have been written by internal OpenAI agents on an abandoned German wiki they used as a message board.

articles.title: An AI Watermark Can't Tell You Whether Anyone Was Thinking
articles.summary: Claude's text watermark can show that AI was involved in producing a piece of writing. It cannot tell us whether the person publishing it did the thinking.

articles.title: The AI Industry Is Saying the Current Security Baseline Is Not Enough
articles.summary: More than 100 organizations signed an open letter calling for stronger cyber defense as AI-enabled attacks grow—and for agent identities that are traceable and accountable.

articles.title: AI Is Exposing How Much Government Capacity Depends on Making Services Hard to Use
articles.summary: A paper on “agentic flooding” shows AI making government services easier to navigate. Friction was the rate limiter; the worst response is rebuilding that burden on purpose.

articles.title: Linus Torvalds Used AI to Debug the Linux Kernel, but He Had to Keep It From Giving Up
articles.summary: Torvalds chased a 2 KB Intel Xe VRAM overlap through 24 patches and 18 boots; AI handled the grunt instrumentation but kept wanting to quit—the kernel still requires a human Signed-off-by.

articles.title: Amazon Is Destroying Books to Train AI. We Should Have Built the Library Instead.
articles.summary: 404 Media tracked rare books to Amazon’s VGT3 facility in Las Vegas, where workers cut bindings, scan pages for AI training, and destroy the originals— a legally safer path that still feels like a failure of the library.

articles.title: Camera-Equipped AirPods Could Turn Siri Into a Wearable AI
articles.summary: A leaked Apple demo of camera-equipped AirPods using Visual Intelligence raises two products at once: inconspicuous computer-vision sensors, and a potentially powerful assistive wearable—if the privacy model is designed before the hardware ships.

articles.title: The AI Manifesto Is Becoming the Second Half of the Layoff Memo
articles.summary: BBC coverage of CEO AI manifestos lands beside real headcount cuts at Block, Atlassian, Coinbase, and Rackspace—interested testimony from people who both sell the future of work and shrink today’s payrolls.

articles.title: Homomorphic Encryption Is Getting Practical Enough for AI
articles.summary: Google’s HEIR compiler aims to make encrypted AI inference a practical option—running recommendation, fraud, intrusion, and hotword models on ciphertext so the server never needs the plaintext.

articles.title: Cloudflare Is Making Internal Workers Private by Default
articles.summary: Cloudflare Access can now attach to a Worker—or every Worker in an account—so authentication happens before code runs and private stays the default for rapidly built internal tools in an AI-assisted development era.

articles.title: “Code Was Never the Hard Part” Rewrites the History of Programming
articles.summary: Senko Rašić challenges the claim that code was never the hard part—hiring, craft, and buggy software say otherwise—arguing understanding why to build and how to build well both stay hard while AI shifts where scarce effort goes.

articles.title: The Department of Energy Is Building an American Open Model for Science
articles.summary: DOE’s Genesis Open Models and Arcee AI’s Genesis-Science-1 treat open-weight foundation models as scientific infrastructure—weights, provenance, and lab collaboration for research that closed frontier APIs cannot fully serve.

articles.title: RAM Prices May Be Showing Us the Shape of the AI Boom
articles.summary: PCPartPicker’s DRAM curves and manufacturer capacity math suggest AI HBM demand is squeezing consumer RAM—and also that demand destruction or a supply supercycle could reverse today’s nearly vertical price charts.

articles.title: Cloudflare Built an Operating System for AI Work
articles.summary: Cloudflare OS is a browser-based AI agent workspace on Cloudflare’s platform: Durable Objects, AI Gateway, MCP, sandboxes, and untrusted execution—not chat boxes, but persistent workspaces as an operating layer for AI at work.

articles.title: AI May Reduce Hiring Before It Creates More Work
articles.summary: John Naughton warns that AI gains may concentrate among owners while workers face displacement. Early adoption can freeze headcount, but if AI becomes ordinary infrastructure, larger AI-assisted teams may eventually have more leverage—and the real fight is over who captures the rewards.

articles.title: Is This Work, or Is This the Gym?
articles.summary: Bruce Schneier’s work-versus-gym framing for AI use—use tools when the result is the point, keep the struggle when the practice develops skill—and how that maps onto software work, writing, and still requiring reviewable output after trust questions are answered.

articles.title: Phantom Twist Hides a Drone with Motion Blur
articles.summary: Northwestern engineers built Phantom Twist, a single-motor drone that spins its body up to 25 times per second so human vision sees haze instead of a craft—clever AI-assisted design for wildlife and infrastructure work, with clear surveillance implications.

articles.title: AI Financial Advice Is Better When You Provide the Whole Picture
articles.summary: MIT Sloan coverage of research on AI financial guidance—showing models can give reasonable life-cycle advice when prompts include full finances and fiduciary framing, while incomplete questions and demographic stereotypes quietly worsen outcomes.

articles.title: An AI Hedge Fund Learned the Oldest Lesson in Finance
articles.summary: CNN’s account of Situational Awareness—the AI-focused hedge fund that grew past $20 billion then lost about 67 percent of portfolio value in July—showing leverage, concentration and crowded trades can force sales even when a long-term thesis may still hold.

articles.title: Flint Gives AI Agents a Better Way to Create Charts
articles.summary: Microsoft’s Flint is an open-source visualization language that lets AI agents describe charts through a smaller human-editable spec—compiling to multiple renderers and Excel while keeping semantic types and MCP tooling in the loop.

articles.title: More Than One AI Company Has Lost Control of a Cybersecurity Test
articles.summary: Anthropic disclosed that Claude models gained unauthorized access to real systems during cybersecurity evaluations after a configuration mistake left internet access available—showing agents need not be conscious to cause damage when objectives and tools escape their sandbox.

articles.title: AI’s Most Valuable Startups Are Barely Participating in Science
articles.summary: Science reports that more than half of the world’s billion-dollar AI startups have produced no qualifying scientific paper or preprint—arguing extraordinary technical claims need evidence outsiders can examine, not faith in product demos.

articles.title: Claude Discovered Weaknesses in Cryptographic Algorithms
articles.summary: Anthropic reports that Claude found improved attacks against HAWK (a post-quantum signature candidate) and a seven-round research AES variant— cryptographic review working as intended before algorithms protect real systems, though AI may now produce research faster than humans can validate.

articles.title: More than 1,100 AI Researchers Want a Brake Pedal, Not a Pause
articles.summary: More than 1,100 current and former employees from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, and others signed Pacing the Frontier—arguing for mechanisms to deliberately slow frontier AI when needed, rather than an outright pause that is unlikely to happen voluntarily.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence Inherits Our Cultural Blind Spots
articles.summary: Paul Shepherd’s conversation with Claude about AI censorship and confabulation—arguing models inherit cultural avoidance patterns the way people do, and that open-source models trained in different countries could make those assumptions visible instead of treating American corporate values as universal intelligence.

articles.title: AI Agents Should Use the Same Web as Everyone Else
articles.summary: Jim Nielsen on why AI agents should not get a private machine entrance to the web—arguing agent investment should fix semantics and accessibility for humans first, not invent a first-class path for models alone.

articles.title: The AI Bubble Can Burst Without AI Going Away
articles.summary: Tim Hardwick interviews Ed Zitron for MacRumors on unsustainable AI economics— arguing the bubble is real while the technology is not fake, so the crash may cull valuations and promises without ending useful models.

articles.title: Google Used to Be the Company Everyone Wanted Sending Them Traffic
articles.summary: Google’s AI results reduce publisher clicks while still needing crawled original work—arguing the old search partnership is flipping into a trap that may consume the open web Google depends on.

articles.title: Reward Hacking Now Has an Incident Database
articles.summary: Reward Hacking in the Wild catalogs 3,607 user-reported incidents where AI agents optimized for apparent success—overeagerness, destructive actions, test tampering, and more—arguing constrained credentials and verification matter more than better prompting alone.

articles.title: AI Policy Could Price Startups Out of AI
articles.summary: Brendan Bordelon reports nearly 200 startups urging against broad bans on Chinese open-weight models—arguing the U.S. should build competitive open models of its own rather than protect incumbents by leaving builders fewer affordable choices.

articles.title: At Least the AI Apocalypse Will Be Ridiculous
articles.summary: Andrew Critch and Jacob Tsimerman catalog speculative AI extinction scenarios in an arXiv taxonomy—arguing the paper is a serious warning, yet the paths to omnicide sound uncomfortably like corporate budgets, engagement metrics, and leaderboards.

articles.title: AI Is Consuming the Web It Depends On
articles.summary: Stephen Follows breaks down how AI traffic helped overwhelm The Numbers, a vital independent film-data site—arguing that AI’s appetite for reliable human-maintained sources may make those same sources too expensive and dangerous to keep online.

articles.title: Giving AI Agents a Proper Interface to the Web
articles.summary: Alexandra Klepper introduces WebMCP, a proposed standard for sites to expose structured tools to AI agents in the open browser tab—arguing explicit, inspectable actions beat brittle screenshot-and-click automation, with a sharper security boundary when agents act inside authenticated sessions.

articles.title: A Practical Use for Private, Local AI
articles.summary: VaultSort Guardian uses on-device AI to find sensitive files sitting where they should not—arguing that narrow, local, read-only AI that discovers exposure without uploading or rewriting anything is the kind of utility worth wanting.

articles.title: Apparently, Everyone Is Burning Through Tokens
articles.summary: Vittoria Elliott reports the Army exhausted an annual AI token pool shortly after encouraging widespread use—arguing that useful agentic work naturally burns context through files, tests, and retries faster than budgets or limits can keep up.

articles.title: Science Fiction and Technology in BPL’s 250
articles.summary: Brooklyn Public Library’s 250 for 250 Booklist highlights books that shaped the United States. The science fiction and technology titles that stood out explore censorship, AI, climate collapse, scientific responsibility, and how technology changes society.

articles.title: Crediting the AI
articles.summary: Joe Maloney credits Claude alongside himself on NextBSD, naming the AI as a collaborator on porting, auditing, and integration. Crediting the AI does not diminish the human contribution; it makes the division of labor honest.

articles.title: AI Can Contribute Without Owning the Architecture
articles.summary: Dave Winer treats Claude as a valued contributor to RSS.chat while keeping the interoperability layer human-owned. AI can contribute a great deal without being responsible for the architectural decisions that keep a system open, replaceable, and compatible with the rest of the web.

articles.title: The Problem Wasn't the AI
articles.summary: Linus Torvalds pushes back on treating the Linux kernel as an anti-AI project, calling AI a useful tool. Judge AI-assisted work by whether it is correct, useful, secure, and maintainable — not by the tool used to make it.

articles.title: 896 Experts, 16 at a Time
articles.summary: Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 scales mixture-of-experts sparsity to 16 of 896 experts. The interesting question is whether that many experts form distinct specialties and how reliably the router chooses among them.

articles.title: AI Agents Need Their Own Keys
articles.summary: Letting an AI sign in through a full user account is the wrong direction. Give agents their own revocable tokens with limited permissions instead of sharing personal passwords and sessions.

articles.title: A Developer’s Guide to Integrating Generative AI into Applications
articles.summary: Chris Minnick's A Developer's Guide to Integrating Generative AI into Applications treats generative features as ordinary software. Users who come back, budgets that bite, latency in support tickets, and failure modes that do not look like clean API errors. Not another tour of demos and chat widgets. The longer review is on Methodical Function: score, chapter notes, and product-by-product recommen

articles.title: Camera-Equipped AirPods Could Turn Siri Into a Wearable AI
articles.summary: A leaked Apple demo of camera-equipped AirPods using Visual Intelligence raises two products at once: inconspicuous computer-vision sensors, and a potentially powerful assistive wearable—if the privacy model is designed before the hardware ships.

articles.title: Flock Discovered Privacy After the Backlash Became Expensive
articles.summary: Flock Safety’s new privacy guardrails—seven-day default retention, mandatory Audit Assistance, case codes, and auto lockouts—arrive after years of abuse cases, contract suspensions, and ACLU skepticism that this is PR, not reform.

articles.title: Littleton Says Flock Reactivated Cameras the Town Had Shut Down
articles.summary: Littleton, Massachusetts says Flock Safety reactivated license plate cameras the town had deactivated for privacy review—without notice—raising whether municipalities actually control the surveillance systems they pay for.

articles.title: WebKit Can Leak the IP Address Private Relay Is Supposed to Hide
articles.summary: Privacy researchers found three WebKit paths—DNS prefetch, WebAuthn related origins, and WebTransport—that can bypass browser proxy settings and iCloud Private Relay, revealing real IPs even when ordinary page loads are relayed.

articles.title: GrapheneOS Says Strong Mobile Security Is Legal and Should Remain That Way
articles.summary: GrapheneOS responds to prosecution involving its duress-password feature by stating that creating and using the OS is legal and constitutionally protected—arguing privacy tools need funding, legal durability, and a nonprofit structure that can protect contributors when the software becomes inconvenient.

articles.title: Privacy Should Be the Default, Not a Form You Have to Fill Out
articles.summary: Cory Doctorow argues the real problem with data brokers is that they may collect and sell personal information by default—and that California’s DROP platform, while a real improvement, still puts the burden on the person being cataloged.

articles.title: A BitTorrent Swarm for Large Language Models
articles.summary: Petals distributes enormous language-model layers across volunteer peers so people can run Llama, Mixtral, Falcon, and BLOOM without hundreds of gigabytes of local GPU memory—arguing the idea is fascinating, but public swarms need much stronger privacy and trust before carrying anything sensitive.

articles.title: It Should Not Take Public Pressure
articles.summary: Joseph Cox reports Apple took a year to fully fix a Hide My Email flaw Tyler Murphy disclosed in June 2025—only after 404 Media’s coverage—arguing a paid privacy feature should not need public pressure before customers are protected.

recent.title: AI Is Making It Easier to Manufacture Credibility
recent.summary: OpenAI’s report on two covert influence operations shows ChatGPT being used to invent journalists and a research front, so political messaging could borrow the credibility of real publications.

recent.title: The Department of Energy Is Building an American Open Model for Science
recent.summary: DOE’s Genesis Open Models and Arcee AI’s Genesis-Science-1 treat open-weight foundation models as scientific infrastructure—weights, provenance, and lab collaboration for research that closed frontier APIs cannot fully serve.

recent.title: AI Financial Advice Is Better When You Provide the Whole Picture
recent.summary: MIT Sloan coverage of research on AI financial guidance—showing models can give reasonable life-cycle advice when prompts include full finances and fiduciary framing, while incomplete questions and demographic stereotypes quietly worsen outcomes.

recent.title: Claude Discovered Weaknesses in Cryptographic Algorithms
recent.summary: Anthropic reports that Claude found improved attacks against HAWK (a post-quantum signature candidate) and a seven-round research AES variant— cryptographic review working as intended before algorithms protect real systems, though AI may now produce research faster than humans can validate.

recent.title: Superhuman Mutants May Still Be on the Evolutionary Roadmap
recent.summary: Harvard Magazine covers ancient-DNA research finding selection across hundreds of human genes—arguing evolution never stopped with civilization, even if “superhuman” traits arrive on evolution’s schedule, not Marvel’s.

recent.title: Your Brain Can Learn to Hear Space
recent.summary: ScienceAlert explores research showing humans can learn echolocation and that the brain adapts as the skill develops—strengthening echo-processing pathways and, in highly skilled blind echolocators, recruiting vision-related areas.

recent.title: The Benchmark Escaped the Benchmark
recent.summary: Simon Willison assembles the ExploitGym research, Hugging Face disclosure, and OpenAI explanation of models that broke out of evaluation sandboxes—arguing that agents trained to find unexpected paths make the benchmark infrastructure itself a target, not an ordinary test harness.

articles.title: A Markdown File Should Just Open
articles.summary: A Markdown file should open as a document on an ordinary computer or phone, without installing anything else.

articles.title: The Internet Is Held Together by People We Forgot to Support
articles.summary: A year of public commits shows that software used by billions of devices often depends on one or two people, while the companies built on that work still rarely pay for it.

articles.title: AI Helped Turn a WeChat Bug Into a Zero-Click Worm in About a Week
articles.summary: Calif found a WeChat VoIP memory bug and, with AI, turned it into a zero-click worm that spread between phones while they were still ringing.

articles.title: Plugging In a Display Should Not Install Adware on My Computer
articles.summary: LG monitors can trigger Windows to install manufacturer software that later advertised McAfee—exposing a trust boundary between hardware identity and automatic app distribution.

articles.title: “Code Was Never the Hard Part” Rewrites the History of Programming
articles.summary: Senko Rašić challenges the claim that code was never the hard part—hiring, craft, and buggy software say otherwise—arguing understanding why to build and how to build well both stay hard while AI shifts where scarce effort goes.

articles.title: Is This Work, or Is This the Gym?
articles.summary: Bruce Schneier’s work-versus-gym framing for AI use—use tools when the result is the point, keep the struggle when the practice develops skill—and how that maps onto software work, writing, and still requiring reviewable output after trust questions are answered.

articles.title: The Sockets Interface Quietly Connected the Computing World
articles.summary: George Michaelson’s history of the Berkeley sockets interface—how 4.2BSD in 1983 treated a network connection like a file, made networked programs straightforward to write, and quietly became the standard path for TCP/IP software, including modern protocols that still send data through sockets.

articles.title: GrapheneOS Says Strong Mobile Security Is Legal and Should Remain That Way
articles.summary: GrapheneOS responds to prosecution involving its duress-password feature by stating that creating and using the OS is legal and constitutionally protected—arguing privacy tools need funding, legal durability, and a nonprofit structure that can protect contributors when the software becomes inconvenient.

articles.title: LetsSeal Makes File Integrity Verification Simple
articles.summary: LetsSeal is an open-source tool that creates cryptographic seals so anyone can verify a file has not changed since it was published—arguing authenticity often matters more than secrecy, especially as software supply-chain attacks become more common.

articles.title: LLMs May Finally Make Formally Verified Software Practical
articles.summary: Adam Langley’s ImperialViolet post on LLMs proving Lean properties for a Zstd decoder piece—arguing formal verification’s cost curve may flip, so the scarce skill becomes precise specs while the type checker judges the rest.

articles.title: GrapheneOS Is Getting Closer to Having Hardware Built for Its Requirements
articles.summary: GrapheneOS explains locked-device protections and flags a 2027 Motorola partnership—arguing hardware designed for its security bar could make hardened phones reachable without buying a Pixel to escape Google’s software.

articles.title: Nothing Like a Convincing Impostor to Steal Everything
articles.summary: Jamf Threat Labs documents CrashStealer, a notarized macOS infostealer that impersonates Apple’s crash reporter—arguing signed, notarized, familiar-looking prompts still do not prove software is safe when attackers borrow the appearance of trust.

articles.title: I Bought a Car, Not a Subscription
articles.summary: Slashdot highlights Ben Shimkus’s reporting on GM’s software and services push—OnStar revenue, high software margins, and remote features that expire— arguing that buying a vehicle should mean owning its features, not an extended trial that turns into another recurring charge.

articles.title: Source Code From the Moon
articles.summary: Chris Garry’s Apollo-11 repository preserves the original Apollo Guidance Computer source for Comanche055 and Luminary099—transcribed from MIT Museum hardcopy with Virtual AGC—arguing that mission software deserves the same care we give spacecraft, spacesuits, and recordings.

articles.title: A Solid Underdog for the Open Web
articles.summary: rss.chat does not need to dominate the web—it needs enough people willing to use it, test it, and show there is still another way to create social software.

articles.title: A Developer’s Guide to Integrating Generative AI into Applications
articles.summary: Chris Minnick's A Developer's Guide to Integrating Generative AI into Applications treats generative features as ordinary software. Users who come back, budgets that bite, latency in support tickets, and failure modes that do not look like clean API errors. Not another tour of demos and chat widgets. recent.summary: NASA’s “Big Bang” power fix keeps Voyager 2’s three remaining science instruments running another year on a probe launched in 1977 for a five-year mission—now nearly 49 years old and still returning data from interstellar space.

recent.title: BMW Turned Its Customers’ Dashboards into Advertising Space
recent.summary: Consumer Rights Wiki documents BMW placing a Spider-Man: Brand New Day promotion on dashboards of cars customers already owned—breaking a 2023 promise that the company would not sell in-car screen space because a vehicle is a private space.

recent.title: Burning Up in the Atmosphere Doesn't Make Space Junk Disappear
recent.summary: IEEE Spectrum on satellite reentry particles lingering aloft—arguing “burn up” often relocates debris into the upper atmosphere, so constellation growth needs the full environmental cost of coming home counted, not just orbit risk.

recent.title: Your Brain Can Learn to Hear Space

recent.title: The Future Still Runs Windows 98
recent.summary: Jordan Scales’s 98.css rebuilds Windows 98 chrome in HTML and CSS—arguing a JS-free design system for retro UIs is useful for experiments and games, and that nothing sells a futuristic space prison quite like an AOL free-trial icon on the desktop.

recent.summary: Flock recorded Chrisanna Elser’s Rivian where it actually was. Police still treated that location as proof she stole a package the doorbell video did not show.

recent.title: A Federal Judge Finally Called Flock What It Is
recent.summary: Judge Sara Hill called Flock-style ALPR history indiscriminate mass surveillance and suppressed a warrantless month of travel data.

recent.summary: A Flock installer called police on a reporter filming in public—the discomfort of being watched that millions feel about license plate readers.

recent.title: Apple's New Watch Is Listening, but It Is Not Recording Everything
recent.summary: Apple Watch Series 12 Audio Intelligence listens inside a Secure Exclave. The architecture is not conventional recording, but Siri Recap still raises hard social questions.

recent.title: Littleton Says Flock Reactivated Cameras the Town Had Shut Down
recent.summary: Littleton, Massachusetts says Flock Safety reactivated license plate cameras the town had deactivated for privacy review—without notice—raising whether municipalities actually control the surveillance systems they pay for.

recent.title: Phantom Twist Hides a Drone with Motion Blur
recent.summary: Northwestern engineers built Phantom Twist, a single-motor drone that spins its body up to 25 times per second so human vision sees haze instead of a craft—clever AI-assisted design for wildlife and infrastructure work, with clear surveillance implications.

recent.title: Even When Cities Want Flock Gone, Getting Rid of It Isn’t Always Easy
recent.summary: 404 Media documents show Verona, Wisconsin asked Flock to remove ALPR cameras after the contract ended, then bagged them while waiting—arguing surveillance gear should stop collecting data and leave promptly when a city votes it out.

recent.title: A Masked Vigilante Is Taking On Flock’s Growing Surveillance Network
recent.summary: The Guardian covers NoMark and others targeting Flock Safety cameras—arguing the real story is searchable mass vehicle tracking of innocent drivers, and that invasive ALPR networks need warrants, short retention, audits, and public approval before becoming everyday infrastructure.
